prompt: During a transfer, the frame's destination MAC address changes several times, while the packet's destination IP address stays the same. Why?
hint: One of the two addresses points at the end of the journey; the other points at its next leg.

choices.text: The MAC addresses the next hop and is rewritten at every leg; the IP addresses the final destination and crosses the whole journey.
choices.why: It is the difference between the address on the envelope and the plate of the truck carrying it right now.

choices.text: The MAC changes because it is drawn at random for each transmission, to make tracking on the local network harder.
choices.why: The MAC is burned into the card. Some systems change it for privacy, but that is optional and does not happen per frame.

choices.text: The IP stays because it is encrypted by TLS and cannot be rewritten by the routers.
choices.why: TLS encrypts the content, not the IP header — which has to stay readable precisely so the packet can be routed.

choices.text: Both are rewritten, but the IP goes back to its original value before reaching the destination.
choices.why: The destination IP is not rewritten on the ordinary path; what does something similar is NAT, and only with the source address.
